item.research_question: How does chemical complexity in single-phase concentrated solid solution alloys (SP-CSAs) affect the migration range and evolution of radiation-induced defects compared to pure nickel under ion irradiation?
item.material_system: Single crystalline pure nickel (Ni), 50%Ni50%Co (NiCo), and 50%Ni50%Fe (NiFe) with fcc structure
item.processing_route: Ion beam irradiation using 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature to fluences of 2 × 10^13/cm^2, ~1 × 10^14/cm^2, and ~5 × 10^15/cm^2; samples prepared via FIB lift-out followed by flash polishing (4% perchloric acid in 96% ethanol, 6~14 V, -30 to -50 °C, 0.05-0.2 s)
item.test_conditions: Room temperature irradiation; cross-sectional TEM (300 keV, g=[200]), RBS-C (3.5 MeV He+ ions), k-ART simulations (300 K and 900 K), and MD simulations (40 keV PKA)
key_findings: Defect clusters in pure Ni stretched to 550 nm at 2 × 10^13/cm^2 and ~1,100 nm at 5 × 10^15/cm^2, exceeding SRIM predictions.
Defect clusters in NiCo and NiFe reached ~460 nm and ~460 nm respectively at low fluence, and ~900 nm and ~800 nm at high fluence.
The damage range in pure Ni was significantly deeper than in NiCo and NiFe at high fluence, indicating higher defect migration rates in pure Ni.
Vacancy-type stacking fault tetrahedra (SFT) and interstitial loops coexist in the same region, consistent with MD simulations.
k-ART simulations showed small vacancy clusters (di-vacancies, tri-vacancies) have migration barriers of 0.3–0.4 eV, making them highly mobile at room temperature.
RBS-C measurements showed damage ranges slightly shallower than TEM (e.g., NiCo: 350 nm vs 460 nm at low fluence) due to density assumptions.
High-fluence irradiation (1.1 × 10^17/cm^2) induced high-level mechanical stress, with implanted Au atoms occupying lattice sites (~7% concentration).
item.mechanism: The extended damage range beyond the theoretical ion stopping depth is attributed to the migration of highly mobile small vacancy clusters and interstitials, prolonged irradiation time allowing further diffusion, and mechanical stress gradients from implanted Au ions driving defects deeper. The slower migration in alloys is caused by higher defect migration barriers due to intrinsic chemical disorder and lattice distortion, which localize energy dissipation and enhance defect recombination.
item.limitations: The text notes that RBS-C depth calculations assume un-irradiated sample density, ignoring potential irradiation-induced volume swelling, and that the 'knee' point method for determining damage range relies on assumptions that may not align perfectly with TEM criteria.
item.future_work: The authors propose that the chemical species of SP-CSA alloys on defect migration should be studied in further detail, particularly by computer simulation.
quotes: Defects in nickel migrate faster than in NiCo and NiFe.
The range of radiation-induced defect clusters far exceed the theoretically predicted depth in all materials after high-dose irradiation.
The slower migration of defects in the alloy along with more localized energy dissipation of the displacement cascade may lead to enhanced radiation tolerance.
